'''Artemas Martin''' (August 3, 1835 – November 7, 1918) was a self-educated American [[mathematician]].<ref>{{MacTutor Biography|id=Martin}}</ref>

==Biography==
Martin  was born on August 3, 1835, in [[Steuben County, New York]], grew up in [[Venango County, Pennsylvania]], and spent most of his life in [[Erie County, Pennsylvania]]. He was home-schooled until the age of 14, when he began studying mathematics at the local school, later moving to the Franklin Select School a few miles away and then to the Franklin Academy, finishing his formal education at age approximately 20. He worked as a farmer, oil driller, and schoolteacher. In 1881, he declined an invitation to become a professor of mathematics at the Normal School in Missouri. In 1885, he became the librarian for the Survey Office of the [[United States Coast Guard]],<ref name="finkel">{{citation|title=A Mathematical Solution Book|first=B. F.|last=Finkel|publisher=Kibler and Company|location=Springfield, MO|year=1902|contribution=Biography: Artemas Martin, M.A., Ph.D., LL.D.|pages=436–437|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ugBDAAAAIAAJ&pg=PA436}}. Reprinted from the ''American Mathematical Monthly'' '''1''' (4): 108–111, 1894.</ref><ref name="nyt">{{citation|title=Mr. A. Martin, of Erie|journal=[[The New York Times]]|date=December 11, 1885|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1885/12/11/archives/mr-a-martin-of-erie.html}}. Reprinted from ''[[The Boston Post]]''.</ref><ref name="science"/><ref name="usons">{{citation|title=Universities and their sons: history, influence and characteristics of American universities, with biographical sketches and portraits of alumni and recipients of honorary degrees, Volume 3|editor-first=Joshua L.|editor-last=Chamberlain|editor-link=Joshua Chamberlain|publisher=R. Herndon company|year=1899|contribution=Martin, Artemas, Yale M.A. (Hon) 1877|pages=201–202|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jzQcAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA201}}.</ref> and in 1898 he became a [[Human computer|computer]] in the Division of Tides.<ref name="science"/> He died on November 7, 1918.<ref name="science">{{citation|title=Artemas Martin|journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]]|year=1918|volume=48|issue=1247|page=508|doi=10.1126/science.48.1247.508|pmid=17795608|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2YkGAQAAIAAJ&pg=PA508|url-access=subscription}}.</ref>

==Mathematical work==
Martin was a prolific contributor of problems and solutions to mathematical puzzle columns in popular magazines beginning at the age of 18 in the ''Pittsburgh Almanac'' and the ''Philadelphia Saturday Evening Post''. From 1870 to 1875, he was editor of the "Stairway Department" of ''Clark's School Visitor'', one of the magazines to which he had previously contributed. From 1875 to 1876 Martin moved to the ''Normal Monthly'', where he published 16 articles on [[diophantine analysis]]. He subsequently became editor of the ''Mathematical Visitor'' in 1877 and of the ''Mathematical Magazine'' in 1882.<ref name="finkel"/><ref name="science"/> In 1893 in Chicago, his paper ''On fifth-power numbers whose sum is a fifth power'' was read (but not by him) at the International Mathematical Congress held in connection with the [[World's Columbian Exposition]].<ref>{{cite book|chapter=''On fifth-power numbers whose sum is a fifth power''|title=Mathematical papers read at the International Mathematical Congress held in connection with the World's Columbian Exposition|year=1896|pages=168–174|location=NY|publisher=Macmillan as publisher for the AMS|url=http://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=uc1.b3841648;view=1up;seq=190}}</ref> He was an Invited Speaker of the [[International Congress of Mathematicians|ICM]] in 1912 in Cambridge UK.<ref>{{cite book|author=Martin, Artemas|chapter=On rational right-angled triangles|title=''In:'' Proceedings of the Fifth International Congress of Mathematicians (Cambridge, 22—25 August 1912)|volume=2|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=1913|pages=40–58|chapter-url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=uc1.31822008115719;view=1up;seq=44}}</ref>

Martin maintained an extensive mathematical library,<ref name="finkel"/><ref name="usons"/> now in the collections of [[American University]].<ref name="science"/><ref name="au">{{citation|url=http://www.american.edu/library/archives/martin.cfm|title=Artemas Martin Collection|publisher=American University|access-date=2011-06-19}}.</ref>

==Awards and societies==
In 1877 Martin was given an honorary M.A. from [[Yale University]].<ref name="finkel"/><ref name="science"/><ref name="usons"/><ref>{{citation|title=Yale's new honorary A.M.|journal=[[Hartford Daily Courant]]|date=July 7, 1877}}.</ref> In 1882 he was awarded another honorary degree, a Ph.D. from [[Rutgers University]], and his third honorary degree, an LL.D., was given to him in 1885 by [[Hillsdale College]].<ref name="finkel"/><ref name="science"/><ref name="usons"/> He was elected to the  [[London Mathematical Society]] in 1878, the [[Société Mathématique de France]] in 1884, the [[Edinburgh Mathematical Society]] in 1885, the [[Philosophical Society of Washington]] in 1886, the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] in 1890, and the [[New York Mathematical Society]] in 1891.<ref name="finkel"/> He was also a member of the [[American Mathematical Society]], the [[Circolo Matematico di Palermo]], the [[Mathematical Association|Mathematical Association of England]], and the [[Deutsche Mathematiker-Vereinigung]].<ref name="usons"/>
